newsitem.title: CHINA: China police on alert after Beijing bus bombing.
newsitem.headline: China police on alert after Beijing bus bombing.

text.p: Beijing police were on high alert on Saturday after an explosion ripped through a public bus in one of the Chinese capital's busiest commercial districts, local sources said.
At least two people were killed when a bomb detonated aboard the bus as it trundled through bustling Xidan district in western Beijing on Friday evening, they said.
State media and police confirmed an explosion had taken place but said it caused no deaths and that it was not yet clear what had caused the blast.
"Yesterday evening at about 7.00 pm (1100 GMT), an explosion occurred on a city Number 22 bus at the Xidan Market stop," the Beijing Daily said in a brief front-page report.
More than 10 passengers were hurt, but none of them sustained life-threatening injuries, a Beijing police spokeswoman said.

The bombing, which followed similar attacks in far-western Xinjiang region but was the first reported in Beijing for many years, prompted authorities to put police on high alert, Chinese sources said.
"The situation is very tense," one source said.
Other sources said a bomb warning had been telephoned to city police before the explosion, but added that the caller had named another area in the capital.
A spate of bus bombings by Moslem separatists in restive Xinjiang last month killed nine people and wounded 74.

Three bombs blew up within minutes of each other on February 25 in the regional capital of Urumqi in attacks apparently timed to coincide with funeral rites in Beijing for paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
Police officials said they had yet to establish what had caused the Beijing explosion, but some city residents were quick to suggest it could also be the work of Xinjiang separatists.

Taxi drivers said their work units had warned them last week not to give rides to any suspicious-looking people from Xinjiang and to be especially cautious in areas where migrant members of the region's dominant Uighur nationality were numerous.
"They said that if we give a Xinjiang person a ride we should check the cab for bombs after he gets out," said one taxi driver, who declined to be identified.
One witness to the Friday explosion said he saw it blow windows out of the back of the articulated bus and that around nine people had appeared to be seriously hurt.
"The bomb blast was not very loud, but it blew out the back window and everybody ran," he said.
"There was a great flame and a 'boom' sound and then people jumped out of the bus," said a young man who had been working nearby.

By Saturday morning all appeared normal in Xidan district, where shoppers flocked into department stores and crowded into restaurants along the main thoroughfare, swept clean of the glass shards that littered it after the blast.
Local shopkeepers working just metres (yards) from the scene of the explosion appeared unconcerned.
"Don't foreign countries also have this kind of incident, with bombs far more serious than this one?" said a shoe shop worker.
